name: Retrieval-Grounded Legal Research
title: Retrieval-Grounded Legal Research
answer: Retrieval-grounded legal research is a method that anchors every answer, summary, or draft to specific passages from primary and secondary legal sources, such as case law, statutes, regulations, and court filings. Instead of relying on a model's general knowledge, the system retrieves relevant text from a curated corpus and cites it in the response. For AI-related matters, this corpus includes the site's 29 AI case law precedents and 142 active AI lawsuits, along with treatises and practice guides. The goal is to reduce hallucination and give a lawyer a verifiable trail from claim to source.

sections.body: Retrieval-grounded legal research is a method that anchors every answer, summary, or draft to specific passages from primary and secondary legal sources, such as case law, statutes, regulations, and court filings. Instead of relying on a model's general knowledge, the system retrieves relevant text from a curated corpus and cites it in the response. For AI-related matters, this corpus includes the site's 29 AI case law precedents and 142 active AI lawsuits, along with treatises and practice guides. The goal is to reduce hallucination and give a lawyer a verifiable trail from claim to source.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The approach runs on a retrieval pipeline connected to a document store of legal texts, typically with embeddings or lexical indexes for search. A large language model then conditions its output on the retrieved passages, often through a prompt that instructs it to quote or cite only from those passages. The site's 732 AI tools and 674 glossary terms can serve as metadata or filtering layers, but the core infrastructure is the index, the retriever, and the generator. No special hardware is required beyond standard cloud inference for the model and vector database.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done in three stages: indexing, retrieval, and grounded generation. First, legal documents are split into passages and stored with citations, jurisdiction, and date. At query time, the retriever finds the most relevant passages, usually a handful, and passes them to the model with the user's question. The model is then constrained to answer using only those passages, and any unsupported statement is either omitted or flagged. A human lawyer reviews the output against the cited sources before it enters a brief or memo.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on citation accuracy, confidentiality, and the limits of machine retrieval. A retrieval-grounded system can still miss a controlling case or misread a passage, so the lawyer remains responsible for verifying every citation. The site's 210 compliance and regulation pages and 6823 state AI bills are frequent retrieval targets, and their rapid change means the index must be updated continuously. Client data entered into a query may be exposed to a third-party model, so firms need clear data handling agreements and should avoid putting privileged material into a public retrieval tool.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The method is moving toward tighter integration with court dockets, real-time legislative feeds, and firm-specific document collections. Future systems will likely retrieve not just text but also prior work product, deposition transcripts, and expert reports, all with persistent citation links. As the site's tracked AI case law grows beyond 29 precedents, retrieval-grounded research will become the default for AI-related litigation and regulatory analysis. The main open problem is evaluating when a retrieved passage is sufficient, so expect more human-in-the-loop review rather than full automation.
